title: GOD SPOKE TO A BOY BECAUSE THE MEN WEARING THE ROBES COULD NO LONGER RECOGNIZE HIS VOICE
paragraphs: GOD SPOKE TO A BOY BECAUSE THE MEN WEARING THE ROBES COULD NO LONGER RECOGNIZE HIS VOICE

The Ultimate Test of Every Christian Teacher — Samuel’s terrifying story is not merely about learning to hear God. It is about what happens when religious familiarity survives after spiritual listening dies.
There is something frightening about 1 Samuel 3 that we have made far too comfortable.
We turn it into a children’s Bible story.
A little boy asleep in the sanctuary.
A voice in the darkness.
“Samuel.”
Tiny feet running toward Eli.
“Here I am.”
A gentle old priest eventually realizing that God is calling the boy.
It sounds beautiful.
Until you read what was happening around him.
Then it becomes terrifying.
Because Samuel was not growing up in a spiritually healthy environment where everyone was eagerly listening to God.
He was serving in the house of the LORD while the priesthood around him was collapsing.
The sons of Eli, Hophni and Phinehas, were priests—and Scripture does not soften its description of them.
“Now the sons of Eli were sons of Belial; they knew not the LORD.” — 1 Samuel 2:12, KJV
Think about that sentence.
They were involved in holy things.
But they did not know the Holy One.
They handled sacrifices.
They occupied religious office.
They stood where worship happened.
They had proximity to the things of God without corresponding submission to God.
And that should frighten every pastor.
Every preacher.
Every Bible teacher.
Every worship leader.
Every Christian content creator.
Every ministry.
Including us.
Because it is possible to become familiar with Christian language while becoming unfamiliar with trembling.
Possible to quote Scripture while resisting what Scripture says.
Possible to speak about God so frequently that people assume we must be walking closely with Him.
Possible to build an audience around Jesus while quietly building an identity around ourselves.
Possible to know how to make people say “Amen” without knowing how to fall on our knees and repent.
And then comes one of the most haunting descriptions of the spiritual atmosphere surrounding Samuel:
“And the word of the LORD was precious in those days; there was no open vision.” — 1 Samuel 3:1, KJV
The Hebrew is striking:
וּדְבַר־יְהוָה הָיָה יָקָר בַּיָּמִים הָהֵם
Udevar-YHWH hayah yaqar bayyamim hahem.
“The word of the LORD was rare/precious in those days.”
The Hebrew word יָקָר — yaqar carries the sense of something precious, costly, valuable, or rare.
God had not ceased to be God.
The sanctuary still existed.
The lamp was still burning.
Religious activity had not disappeared.
But the word of the LORD was rare.
That is the nightmare.
Not an empty church.
A functioning religious system in which hearing from God has become rare.
Not atheists openly rejecting God.
Religious people becoming so accustomed to holy things that they no longer tremble when God speaks.
And somewhere inside that darkness was Samuel.
Young.
Inexperienced.
Still learning.
Scripture is careful with the details.
“Now Samuel did not yet know the LORD, neither was the word of the LORD yet revealed unto him.” — 1 Samuel 3:7, KJV
The Hebrew says:
וּשְׁמוּאֵל טֶרֶם יָדַע אֶת־יְהוָה
UShmu’el terem yada et-YHWH.
“Samuel had not yet known the LORD.”
That matters.
Samuel was not some spiritual celebrity walking around announcing that he had superior revelation.
He did not even understand what was happening.
When God called him, Samuel thought Eli was calling.
So he ran to Eli.
“Here am I; for thou calledst me.”
Eli said he had not.
Samuel returned to bed.
God called again.
Samuel ran back.
Again Eli sent him away.
Then it happened again.
Three times.
And here is where the story becomes painfully relevant to Christian leadership.
The boy could hear the voice.
But he did not yet recognize the Speaker.
The older priest did not initially hear the call.
But eventually he recognized what was happening.
This is important because Eli should not be caricatured beyond what Scripture actually says.
The biblical text does not simply say, “Eli had completely stopped listening to God.”

His spiritual condition was undeniably compromised. His household was under judgment. His sons were corrupt. His eyesight was failing, and the narrative is filled with imagery of dimness and declining leadership. Yet Eli still possessed enough spiritual awareness to discern that the LORD was calling Samuel.
And what Eli did next gives us one of the greatest tests of a true spiritual teacher.
He did not tell Samuel:
“Listen to me.”
He taught Samuel to answer God.
He did not make himself the destination.
He pointed the boy beyond himself.
“Therefore Eli said unto Samuel, Go, lie down: and it shall be, if he call thee, that thou shalt say, Speak, LORD; for thy servant heareth.” — 1 Samuel 3:9, KJV
Then God came.
“Samuel, Samuel.”
And Samuel answered:
דַּבֵּר כִּי שֹׁמֵעַ עַבְדֶּךָ
Dabber ki shomea avdekha.
“Speak, for Your servant is listening.”
Do not rush past that.
Listening in Scripture is not merely sound entering an ear.
The Hebrew verb שָׁמַע — shama can carry the intertwined ideas of hearing, listening, and responding obediently.
Samuel was not saying:
“Speak, Lord, because I would like some interesting religious information.”
His posture was:
Speak.
Your servant is listening.
Your servant.
That changes everything.
Because the ultimate test of Christian teaching is not whether a teacher can make people fascinated with the teacher.
It is whether the teaching drives people toward faithful submission to God as He has revealed Himself in Scripture and ultimately in Jesus Christ.
That test is desperately needed now.
We live in an age where charisma can masquerade as anointing.
Confidence can masquerade as authority.
Popularity can masquerade as fruit.
Emotional intensity can masquerade as truth.
A viral clip can travel around the world before anyone asks whether the person speaking has handled Scripture faithfully.
And perhaps even more dangerously, Christians can become so attached to a personality that questioning the teacher begins to feel like questioning God.
That is not discipleship.
That is dangerous.
A faithful Christian teacher does not fear biblical examination.
A faithful teacher invites it.
The Bereans were praised because they received Paul’s preaching eagerly while still searching the Scriptures daily “whether those things were so” (Acts 17:11).
Imagine that.
They checked Paul.
The apostle Paul.
And Scripture calls them noble for doing it.
John writes:
Paul goes even further:
“But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed.” — Galatians 1:8, KJV
Even “we.”
Paul includes himself in the test.
That is astonishing humility before the Gospel.
The message stands above the messenger.
The Gospel judges the preacher.
The preacher does not get to rewrite the Gospel.
And the Greek word Paul uses in Galatians 1:8 is devastating:
ἀνάθεμα — anathema.
Accursed.
Paul is essentially saying that no reputation, supernatural appearance, impressive messenger, apostolic credential, or spiritual experience has authority to replace the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
Not even an angel from heaven.
So why would we surrender our discernment to a microphone?
Why would we give a YouTube channel what Scripture would not give an angel?
Why would we believe something merely because a preacher says, “God told me”?
Test it.
Test us.
Test every Christian page you follow.
Test every sermon.
Test every prophecy.
Test every viral Christian video.
Test every devotional.
Test every article.
Test every teacher you admire.
Not with cynicism.
With Scripture.
Because a teacher who genuinely loves you should want you anchored more deeply in Jesus than in them.
And there is another side of Samuel’s story we cannot escape.
God’s first recorded message to Samuel was not easy.
It was judgment against Eli’s house.
Imagine being young Samuel.
You finally recognize the voice of God.
And the first message you must carry is one you desperately wish you did not have to deliver.
The next morning, Samuel was afraid to tell Eli.
Of course he was.
Truth can cost something.
And this exposes another test of teachers.
What happens when Scripture says something our audience does not want to hear?
What happens when biblical truth threatens engagement?
What happens when repentance is less marketable than affirmation?
What happens when Jesus’ words confront the very people whose approval we crave?
Do we soften the truth until nobody needs the cross anymore?
Do we preach blessing without repentance?
Destiny without holiness?
Healing without surrender?
Grace without truth?
A crown without a cross?
A Christianity where Jesus becomes an accessory to the life we already wanted?
Samuel had to speak.
And the Christian teacher must speak too.
But here is where the Gospel changes the entire picture.
Because Christianity is not ultimately the story of good listeners earning their way back to God.
It is the story of God coming for people who repeatedly refused to listen.
People like Israel.
People like Eli’s sons.
People like Peter.
People like you.
People like me.
We have all had moments when God’s Word confronted something we wanted to keep.
And we negotiated.
Delayed.
Rationalized.
Hid.
Maybe nobody knows what you are carrying right now.
Maybe your Christian vocabulary is intact.
Your Bible app is still on your phone.
You still post verses.
You still say “God bless.”
You still know exactly when to lift your hands during worship.
But somewhere underneath all of it, there is a room in your heart you keep locked when Jesus approaches.
A relationship.
An addiction.
Bitterness.
Pornography.
Pride.
Envy.
Secret messages.
Dishonesty.
A private compromise.
An unforgiven wound you have turned into permission to hate.
A hunger for attention.
A religious reputation you are terrified of losing.
And perhaps the most dangerous prayer you could pray tonight is the prayer Samuel learned:
Speak, Lord.
Your servant is listening.
Because what if He puts His finger exactly where you hoped He would not?
What if the Scripture you have been avoiding is precisely the Scripture you need?
What if repentance is waiting on the other side of your excuses?
But listen carefully.
Jesus does not expose sin because He enjoys destroying sinners.
He exposes darkness to bring us into light.
The cross proves it.
At Calvary, God did not pretend sin was harmless.
He revealed how devastating sin truly is.
And then the sinless Son of God bore judgment for sinners.
Jesus Christ “bare our sins in his own body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24).
He was crucified.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
That means the answer to your scandal is not better image management.
It is Jesus.
The answer to your hidden life is not pretending harder.
It is Jesus.
The answer to religious hypocrisy is not abandoning Christ because religious people failed you.
It is coming to the Christ whom hypocrites themselves desperately need.
The Gospel does not say, “Clean yourself until Jesus can tolerate you.”
The Gospel calls sinners to repent and believe.
Grace does not tell us sin does not matter.
Grace tells us sin mattered so much that Christ went to the cross—and that His mercy is so astonishing that repentant sinners can be forgiven, cleansed, adopted, and transformed.
Maybe you have spent years thinking your scandal disqualifies you forever.
Ask Peter.
He denied Jesus.
Three times.
And the risen Christ came looking for him.
Peter's failure was real.
So was Christ's restoration.
Jesus did not rewrite history by pretending Peter never fell.
He rewrote Peter’s future through grace.
That is what Jesus does.
He takes people whose worst chapter looked like the ending and writes redemption where shame expected a grave.
Not because scandal is insignificant.
Because Jesus is greater.
And perhaps this is the sentence you needed before closing this article:
You do not need another Christian personality to become your spiritual substitute for Jesus.
You need Jesus.
You need His Word.
You need the Gospel.
You need repentance.
You need grace.
You need the Holy Spirit producing fruit that no algorithm can manufacture.
And you need faithful believers who will keep pointing you back to Christ when your heart starts wandering.
That is the kind of community Gospel Warrior desires to help build.
Not people dependent upon us.
People becoming increasingly dependent upon Christ.
Not an audience impressed by religious content.
Disciples hungry for biblical truth.
So test what you read here.
Open 1 Samuel 2 and 3 yourself.
Read Acts 17.
Read Galatians 1.
Read 1 John 4.
Search the Scriptures.
And if something we publish cannot survive the Bible, choose the Bible.
Every time.
If God has been restoring you after failure, tell somebody what His grace has done.
Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded believer needed to survive tonight.
Not because sharing a Gospel Warrior article earns favor with God.
It does not.
It cannot.
We glorify God through faith in Christ expressed in lives of worship, obedience, love, generosity, truth, and good works—not by purchasing access to a ministry.

But if this ministry is helping you grow closer to Jesus, you can glorify God with your resources by freely choosing to support Gospel work, just as Christians may freely support faithful ministry, and you can help put biblical truth in front of someone who may never walk through a church door.
Sometimes sharing is more than clicking a button.
Sometimes it is placing truth where a hurting friend can stumble across it at 2:13 in the morning.
There may come a day when a charismatic voice says exactly what you desperately want to hear, and you will need to remember:
Test the teacher.
Test the message.
Open the Bible.
Follow Jesus.
Not for us.
For the person who is still lying awake in the darkness wondering whether God can speak into their mess.
For the Christian who has mistaken familiarity with religion for intimacy with Jesus.
For the wounded believer who needs permission to test human teachers without abandoning Christ.
For the secret sinner convinced that exposure means the end.
For the person whose scandal seems louder than grace.
Tell them.
Jesus still saves.
Jesus still forgives.
Jesus still restores.
Jesus still calls sinners out of darkness.
And Jesus is still writing stories that shame thought were already finished.
Samuel heard his name in the darkness.
Maybe tonight, through the written Word of God, you are being reminded of yours.
The question is not whether you can surround yourself with enough religious noise.
The question is whether, when Scripture confronts your heart, you are willing to whisper:
דַּבֵּר כִּי שֹׁמֵעַ עַבְדֶּךָ
Speak, for Your servant is listening.
Because the most dangerous spiritual condition may not be having nothing to say about God.
It may be having so much to say about Him that you no longer stop long enough to obey Him.
And the most beautiful beginning may be the moment all your excuses finally become quiet enough for repentance to answer.
Never become so familiar with the things of God that you can stand beside His lamp and no longer tremble at His voice.
